item.title: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
item.description: A lawsuit challenges Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's effort to commute all 548 death sentences, citing failures to notify district attorneys.
item.content:encoded:
A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release.

Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES

"The death penalty remains on the books in California, and as you alluded to, California voters have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish the death penalty," Smith said. "So Californians understand that it can be an appropriate punishment in certain circumstances. Now, [Gov.] Newsom, he does have the ability to exercise the pardon, the commutation power, the contours of that obviously are being litigated, but I think what's clear is that from a practical standpoint, [Gov.] Newsom is essentially using this to circumvent the clear will of the voters and impose his own views of the death penalty over those of ... the California populace."

"Now some of the specifics related to this suit challenging Gavin Newsom's use of the commutation pardon, that is going to vary a little bit from state to state," Smith added. "So this is going focus largely on issues of California state law and the issues specifically that I think will get the most attention is whether the California Supreme Court would essentially have to weigh in and more or less approve some of these repeat offenders before their sentences can be commuted."

California voters notably defeated Proposition 34, a ballot initiative to ban capital punishment, in 2012, according to Ballotpedia. Voters in the Golden State similarly rejected Proposition 62, the Abolition of Death Penalty Measure, in November 2016, per Ballotpedia.

The lawsuit alleges that Newsom "has claimed to himself the unfettered power to decide how clemency should be granted, ignored the Legislature’s requirement of a referral to the Board of Parole Hearings for investigation and recommendation, ignored the role of the trial court and District Attorney in providing crucial factual input to the Board of Parole Hearings, ignored the limitation of the required notice to District Attorneys, and deprived the Legislature, the public, and this Court of the information needed to determine whether he has abused his authority."

CJLF's lawsuit also requests that "the Court immediately stay any issuance, implementation, recognition, or enforcement of the challenged commutations pending further order of the Court and pending determination of this petition on the merits."

Anne Marie Schubert, president and CEO of CJLF, said in a statement that the lawsuit "is about protecting the constitutional rights of victims, defending the rule of law, and ensuring that no Governor is above the law."

"The Governor’s clemency power does not authorize mass commutations that disregard constitutional safeguards, legally required procedures, or victims’ rights," Schubert said, adding that "blanket commutation is not an exercise of discretion — it is an abandonment of it."

CJLF and Newsom's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The coalition suing Newsom is comprised of several law enforcement leaders and organizations, victims’ rights groups and multiple district attorneys, including Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho, who ran as a Democrat in the 2026 congressional primary.

Some of California’s most notorious serial killers are among the death row inmates whose sentences Newsom plans to commute, KTLA reported Nov. 8.

"Obviously, these are individuals who, again, have been convicted by a jury of their peers of committing particularly aggravated forms of murder," Smith told Fox News Digital. "Again, many of these individuals tortured their victims and included sexual violence against their victims before they were ultimately killed. And so these are individuals that their own peers thought deserved the death penalty. And, so again, to see [Gov.] Newsom circumventing this through his commutation power is very, very troubling."

Under the California Constitution, Newsom must obtain a recommendation from at least four California Supreme Court justices before commuting the sentences of 382 inmates who have been convicted of more than one felony.

The California Supreme Court has invited interested parties to weigh in on the proposed commutations, with legal briefs due Nov. 24 and Newsom's response due Dec. 4. Attorney General Rob Bonta told the court Newsom will not formally commute any death sentences until the justices act, including those of inmates with only one felony conviction.

Newsom's office has argued that the governor's broad constitutional clemency authority allows him to initiate blanket commutations without following statutory procedures governing individual applications, while separately seeking the California Supreme Court's required recommendation for inmates with multiple felony convictions.

CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

"District attorneys have a legal responsibility to represent the people of California and protect the rights of crime victims," Greg Totten, CEO of the California District Attorneys Association, said in a statement. "The Governor’s failure to provide legally required notice to prosecutors has deprived them of the opportunity to provide critical information and ensure that victims and their families are heard."

'BABY KILLERS, COP KILLERS' HAVE AN ALLY IN NEWSOM, MURDERED GIRL'S FATHER SAYS AMID DEATH ROW CONTROVERSY

"No Governor should be permitted to circumvent the very safeguards designed to ensure that justice is served," Totten added.

Newsom's proposed commutations would mark the largest mass commutation of death sentences in American history, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Newsom also issued a March 2019 executive order establishing a moratorium on executions in California, leaving the state's death penalty law and existing death sentences in place.

Democratic California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra said in a May 28, 2026 X post that he plans to extend California’s moratorium on executions when he takes office.

"Governor Newsom’s death penalty moratorium represented an important step toward a more just criminal justice system," Becerra wrote in the post. "As Governor, I will extend California’s moratorium on executions and continue moving our state away from a costly, flawed system that disproportionately impacts Black and brown communities and too often gets it wrong."

Dan Dow, district attorney of San Luis Obispo County, California, blasted Newsom's proposed commutation as "a sickening abuse of power" in a Nov. 5 statement.

"Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California's 548 condemned killers that the killers' lives matter more," Dow asserted. "Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power."

item.title: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal
item.description: Investors behind a False Claims Act qui tam lawsuit over Crescent Dunes' $275 million federal grant say the Trump DOJ is defending a Biden-era dismissal.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.

Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

The investors allege that companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.

REGULATORS ALLOW OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT TO KILL THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY, INVESTIGATION FINDS

The plant was built around an emerging solar technology that used thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a towering receiver, heating molten salt that could be stored and used to generate electricity even after sunset.

In 2020, a group of private investors who had put $90 million into the project and suffered substantial losses filed a whistleblower lawsuit, alleging the companies had misled the federal government to secure the enormous grant.

But in November 2024, just two days after Trump's reelection, Biden's Justice Department moved to shut down the lawsuit, arguing that pursuing the case would burden federal agencies.

WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES

The incoming Trump administration could have reconsidered that position in early 2025. Instead, its Justice Department defended the Biden-era dismissal in an April filing with a federal appeals court.

CMB, an investment group headed by Pat Hogan, is appealing the dismissal. Hogan is also urging Trump’s Justice Department to ask the court to reopen the case.

"It makes no sense," Hogan told Fox News Digital in a video interview.

Hogan said he had contacted Trump's Justice Department seeking help reviving the case but had received no commitment.

"The real problem here is, why isn't the government asking for this?" he said. "All in all, I would say this has just been a fleecing of the federal government by a foreign entity. And we have the opportunity to fix it, and they're doing nothing."

Hogan argues that allowing the lawsuit to proceed could potentially net hundreds of millions of dollars for taxpayers.

Under the False Claims Act, which CMB used to bring its lawsuit, companies found liable can face damages of up to three times the government's proven losses, plus additional penalties.

"This could be a billion dollars," Hogan said.

Tonopah Solar Energy, the plant's former owner and one of the defendants, has rejected CMB's allegations as baseless in court filings. Other companies named in the lawsuit have also backed the Justice Department's effort to dismiss the case.

In an April 2026 court filing, Trump's Justice Department defended the Biden administration's decision, making the same argument that continuing the lawsuit would drain government resources and that federal law gave it broad authority to shut down the case. In court filings reviewed by Fox News Digital, neither administration put a dollar figure on the cost of continuing the lawsuit.

The decision has left Hogan and his investors questioning why the government shut down the case — and what Treasury officials knew about the plant's serious problems when they approved the $275 million grant.

At the heart of the lawsuit is a dispute over whether Crescent Dunes was properly completed — and whether its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, was entitled to collect the $275 million Treasury grant.

The grant was part of a $26 billion program within the Obama administration's broader $90 billion green-energy push, launched under the 2009 economic stimulus package to create jobs and turbocharge its green energy agenda.

Known as Section 1603, the program paid developers about 30% of their qualifying construction costs once their facilities were "placed in service" — meaning ready and available for their intended use. Treasury considered several factors in determining whether a plant met that standard, including whether it had passed critical tests, begun generating electricity and come under its owner's control.

Crescent Dunes began generating electricity in 2015, but CMB alleges it had produced no more than 32% of its expected output through June 2016.

Then, in October 2016, a failure involving the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank shut it down for months.

In December, while Crescent Dunes was still shut down, its builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, formally handed the plant over to its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, under an arrangement known as "provisional acceptance."

But first, they changed the construction contract to allow the handover despite major defects and unfinished repairs.

That agreement came just days before the year-end deadline for solar plants to be ready for use to qualify for the Treasury grants.

In a later court filing, CMB alleged that more than 9,000 defects had been identified and grouped into roughly 500 outstanding construction items, including seven major deficiencies. The investors argue the problems showed the plant was not ready to be handed over.

The December agreement itself acknowledged that repairs to the failed hot molten-salt storage tank were still needed. The tank was central to the plant's operation, storing heat from the sun so electricity could be generated even after sunset.

CMB alleges the companies used the revised agreement to make Crescent Dunes appear ready for use and secure the Treasury grant, even though major problems remained unresolved.

Records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Treasury had questioned whether Crescent Dunes was ready for use months before approving the grant payment.

In September 2016, Treasury questioned a claim by Tonopah Solar Energy that Crescent Dunes had been ready for use since February of that year. The agency pointed to a July commissioning report suggesting the builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, had not yet formally handed control of the facility over to Tonopah.

In a Sept. 21 response to Treasury's questions, Tonopah Solar Energy defended its claim, arguing that the plant had passed key tests and was capable of generating electricity. It also acknowledged an earlier extended shutdown caused by problems with the plant's salt-piping system.

The following month, the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank failed, forcing the plant offline for months.

Despite that breakdown, Tonopah and Cobra went ahead with the revised handover agreement in December.

On March 7, 2017, just weeks into the first Trump administration, Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment — even though Crescent Dunes remained shut down nearly five months after the tank failure.

The plant would not resume generating electricity until July 2017.

The approval letter said Treasury was still reviewing some of the project's claimed costs before deciding whether to release additional money.

In February 2018, Treasury approved an additional $31.9 million, bringing the total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million, according to newly obtained federal records. The additional payment was scheduled for disbursement within seven business days.

But Treasury was not the only federal agency involved.

The Department of Energy, which had backed Crescent Dunes with a $737 million federal loan guarantee, also had a say in major construction decisions. DOE approved the revised December handover despite unfinished repairs. It also waived certain missed deadlines, allowing the plant to be formally recognized as operational under its loan agreement.

That approval did not automatically qualify Crescent Dunes for the separate Treasury grant.

A separate December 2016 financing agreement involving Tonopah Solar Energy and DOE required the Treasury grant money to go first toward repaying the project’s short-term federal borrowing, including principal and accrued interest.

Documents obtained by Fox News Digital show that Tonopah Solar Energy made a $218.9 million payment toward a federal loan in March 2017, shortly after Treasury approved its initial grant award.

"So in a sense, the federal government just paid themselves, right? So they're still out the money, right," Hogan told Fox News Digital.

On April 12, 2017, while Crescent Dunes was still offline, DOE published an article celebrating the plant as a breakthrough in solar technology without mentioning that it had been shut down for months.

What remains unclear is whether Treasury officials knew about the October breakdown, unfinished repairs and December contract changes when they authorized the initial grant payment — information that could have affected whether the plant qualified for the grant.

Fox News Digital has asked DOE and Treasury about the grant's approval process, the plant's condition and taxpayer losses, but neither agency has provided a full accounting.

In a statement, the Trump administration's Department of Energy criticized previous administrations' handling of the project, saying it had resolved its financial interests in Crescent Dunes in 2020.

"It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green New Scam," a DOE spokesperson said. "Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project."

Fox News Digital has also filed Freedom of Information Act requests seeking grant payment records, loan accounting and communications between the agencies.

In January 2020, Hogan's investment group, CMB, which had lent $90 million to a company tied to Crescent Dunes developer SolarReserve, sued Tonopah Solar Energy and companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, accusing them of defrauding the federal government.

The lawsuit was filed under the False Claims Act, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on the government's behalf and receive a share of any money recovered. Known as "qui tam" cases, the lawsuits can be taken over or dismissed by the Justice Department.

After investigating CMB's allegations for more than three years, Biden's Justice Department declined to take over the lawsuit in June 2023, leaving CMB to pursue it alone.

On Nov. 7, 2024, just two days after Trump's election victory, Biden's Justice Department moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that continuing the case would burden the Treasury, Energy and Justice departments.

CMB challenged the move, arguing that Biden's DOJ had failed to explain what had changed since it allowed the investors to proceed.

Then, in July 2025, six months into Trump's second term, a federal judge granted DOJ's request and dismissed the lawsuit without deciding whether the fraud allegations were true.

CMB appealed to the Ninth Circuit, where Trump's Justice Department defended the dismissal in an April 2026 court filing.

Matt Dunn, an attorney at Covington & Burling who specializes in False Claims Act litigation, described DOJ's decision to intervene after initially allowing the case to proceed as "unusual, but not extraordinary."

Dunn said the government may have its own assessment of a lawsuit's potential value that differs from the whistleblower's.

"The government might privately have a different view of the merits of the case or the potential value of the case that it doesn't necessarily share publicly," Dunn said.

Dunn said the Supreme Court has given the government substantial discretion to dismiss such cases, describing the legal hurdle for whistleblowers seeking to overturn a dismissal as "an extraordinarily high bar for a relator to overcome."

Hogan, meanwhile, has a financial stake in the outcome. He says his investors lost the $90 million they lent to the SolarReserve-linked company.

If the lawsuit is revived and CMB ultimately succeeds, the government theoretically could recover up to three times its proven damages under the False Claims Act, and CMB could receive a share, potentially offsetting its investors' losses.

"That's my job for my investors to leave no stone unturned to try to make sure that, in fact, I get their money back," Hogan said.

The Ninth Circuit must now decide whether the lawsuit can move forward — potentially opening the door for the government to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed funds — or whether DOJ's decision to shut it down will stand.

The Justice Department's handling of the case has also drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit.

Gooden later urged Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to consider suspending federal contracts with companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, whose subsidiary Cobra built the plant and held a stake in Tonopah Solar Energy. He also called for an investigation into ACS and Banco Santander's roles in the project's financing and bankruptcy amid the allegations of fraud involving federal funds.

"When taxpayers are defrauded to a scale this massive, our government has a responsibility to get the facts and hold those responsible to account," Gooden told Fox News Digital. "That is why I have asked Secretary Hegseth to pause contracts with ACS-affiliated entities until these allegations are fully reviewed and every avenue to recover taxpayer money has been pursued."

One such contract involves a $2.84 billion Navy dry dock project at Pearl Harbor awarded to a joint venture involving ACS subsidiary Dragados. The project completion date has been delayed from September 2027 to March 2029, according to the Government Accountability Office. Dragados is not accused of fraud in the Crescent Dunes lawsuit.

Miller, meanwhile, also questioned how a project backed by nearly $1 billion in federal financing could end up selling for $7 million.

"That's not good math," Miller told Fox News Digital. She suggested another congressional letter could be warranted, saying that "if we can recover any of that taxpayer money, that would be wonderful."

In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead.

In a July 10 response obtained by Fox News Digital, DOJ revealed that Crescent Dunes was one of just 12 cases in which it moved to shut down a lawsuit after initially allowing it to proceed — fewer than 0.3% of nearly 5,000 whistleblower cases received between 2020 and 2025.

DOJ also confirmed that other federal agencies can push to have such lawsuits dismissed, including to avoid the burden of producing evidence. But it did not say whether Treasury or DOE pushed to kill the Crescent Dunes case — or what investigators found when they examined the fraud allegations.

The companies accused of fraud have backed DOJ's effort to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that federal law gives the government broad authority to shut down whistleblower cases.

Tonopah Solar Energy, which filed for bankruptcy in January 2026, has also fiercely rejected CMB's allegations, accusing the investors of pursuing a "scorched earth mission" through repeated legal challenges against the company.

"The reality is there is no merit to CMB's claims whatsoever," the company argued in an April 2026 bankruptcy filing.

Tonopah Solar Energy made those arguments while winding down its affairs in bankruptcy, before selling the plant's assets in July. The new owners had no involvement in the alleged 2016 fraud, and the bankruptcy sale generally shielded them from the former owner's legal liabilities.

In a separate 2020 lawsuit, Hogan's investors sought to recover an allegedly unpaid $90 million loan, suing companies tied to Crescent Dunes after SolarReserve failed to repay much of the money. They suffered a setback in 2024 when an arbitration panel rejected five of their claims and ordered them to pay $2.44 million in legal fees and costs.

The companies did not respond to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment.

The dispute was separate from the whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving the $275 million Treasury grant.

Despite years of investigation, the Justice Department has never publicly disclosed what it uncovered.

Nearly seven years after Hogan's investors filed their lawsuit, the fraud allegations have never been tested at trial. And despite President Trump's pledge to crack down on fraud and wasteful green-energy spending, his Justice Department is still defending the Biden administration's decision to shut down the case.

"If we're wrong, the evidence will show it," Hogan said. "But don't let a Biden-era dismissal prevent the merits from ever being heard."

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Listen to Jonathan before you gobble turkey with Trump-hating loved ones
item.description: Psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert says Americans fear facing their Trump loving uncle at Thanksgiving dinner, with some considering sitting out the holiday.
item.content:encoded:
Every two years, Thanksgiving, that most American of holidays, falls just a few weeks after a major national election, and it can be a dicey mixture of loud voices, hurt feelings and anger.

Especially in the age of Trump.

"A few weeks ago I started seeing patients who are concerned about the upcoming holiday," psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital. "They are concerned about how they will deal with their Trump-loving uncle or their blue-haired cousin. Some have talked about sitting out the holiday, which I don’t think is the answer."

LEE CARTER: THE BIGGEST WINNER OF THIS ELECTION IS NOT WHO YOU THINK

DAVID MARCUS: TRUMP DERANGEMENT SYNDROME ISN'T MENTAL ILLNESS, IT'S MASS HYSTERIA

Polling data backs up what Alpert is seeing on the couch, as do conversations this columnist has had with Americans who have lost relationships over politics in the past decade or so.

According to a 2026 UC Irvine poll, between 26-37% of people have had relationships irreparably harmed by politics. Honestly, the figure seems a bit low to me, as almost everyone I have spoken with, and it's a lot of people, say the red vs blue wars have at least strained some friendships.

5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

‘NO CONTACT’ ON THE RISE: NEARLY 2 IN 5 AMERICANS CUT TIES WITH LOVED ONES

What is curious about this phenomenon is that, while political arguments over a holiday meal have been all but a cliche for decades in the United States, it is only over the past 10 years or so that we have seen, in a widespread way, people cutting others out of their lives over the political and social turmoils of the day.

Alpert, who has made quite a study of Trump Derangement Syndrome, lays the cause, if not the blame of our current, cantankerous condition at the feet of the president.

THERAPY CULTURE IS TURNING POLITICS INTO A NATIONAL NERVOUS BREAKDOWN

"When Trump entered politics, that's when I started to see this polarization reach this point of cutting off relatives," he said. "Prior to Trump, I never saw it."

To understand how a healthy society can come to such a place, it is useful to look at examples of the phenomenon from the past.

In 1790, Compte Roger de Demas had returned to a Paris on the verge of revolution after several years abroad in the military. His description of what he found feels eerily familiar: "Conversation had become habitually serious and profound, and the grace and geniality that used to constitute its charm had altogether vanished; the conflict of opinions had killed all confidence and intimacy … Society had generated into factions, conversation into debate, and pleasures into a mere means of distraction. Everything was subservient to the question of public affairs."

Alpert noted this myopic attitude towards politics as well, saying of those immune to it, "They … have more that they care about in their life than politics, maybe they’ve got families or careers or hobbies, or sports, they have more going on in their lives. It's the people who give politics top priority, those are the people who are suffering."

WHY WE STARTED EXPECTING LEADERS TO MANAGE OUR FEELINGS

And who often make those around them suffer with their constant droning from either political side.

We do have to ask, on the other side of the etiquette ledge, if we lose something when families and friends can’t discuss the issues of the day, or feel the need to censor themselves.

KENNEDY FAMILY RIFT OVER RFK JR IS 'DEVASTATING,' SAYS TIM SHRIVER AS HE URGES AMERICANS TO CHOOSE DIGNITY

For Alpert, at least for now, this seems like a sacrifice we have to make.

"If we get back to a time when people could just have spirited debates and heated discussions and not to the point where they demonize their Republican uncle, just because he’s a Republican, then sure, I’m all for that. But we’ve gotten to such a dangerous place where we are calling people, ‘Hitler,’ or ‘evil.’"

UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT SOUNDS ALARM AS NEARLY HALF OF STUDENTS JUSTIFY VIOLENCE TO STOP 'HATE SPEECH'

I'M JESSICA TARLOV, AND SOMETIMES I GET IT WRONG. ACCEPTING THAT IS THE FIRST STEP TOWARDS BETTER DEBATES

It would be nice to get back to that time, and perhaps we can hope that two years from now, without Trump on the ballot literally or figuratively anymore, we can return to the old rhetorical normal.

For normalcy to return, however, for old relationships to be mended and new ones to never again be cut asunder, it will take more than the mere absence of Trump, even if he was the catalyst of our season of discontent. Rather, it is a choice we must all make to listen more and judge less.

AHEAD OF AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY, FAITH GROUP URGES FAMILIES TO RECONNECT THROUGH PATRIOTIC TRADITIONS

All of us can help to bring grace, geniality and charm back to the Thanksgiving table starting this year, not necessarily by avoiding politics, but by being reminded, by the warm hearth of home that there is much, much more to life.

item.title: Newsom and Biden overruled thousands of jurors with the stroke of a pen
item.description: Gavin Newsom spared 548 California death row inmates on Nov. 5. He waited till he had one foot out the door.
item.content:encoded:
Not all murders are eligible for the death penalty. In fact, murder alone is almost never sufficient for society’s ultimate punishment. It must be murder plus what we call an aggravating circumstance, such as the murder of more than one person, the murder of a child or a murder in the commission of another crime, such as burglary, rape or robbery.

In the universe of capital-eligible cases, very few death sentences are sought and even fewer are given. For those given, the process is rightfully arduous. The prosecution must convince the jury of both the underlying crimes and that death is the proper sentence. Those are separate trials. In other words, 12 people must agree, beyond a reasonable doubt, twice before anyone can be sentenced to death. And the return of the death verdict is only the beginning of the appellate process. There are direct appeals, collateral appeals and challenges to everything the police, prosecutors, defense attorneys and judges do and say.

And even though I handled seven death penalty cases to verdict, I full well understand those who are opposed to capital punishment and have spent no time trying to change their minds.

To serve on a death penalty jury, each potential juror is questioned individually about his or her beliefs, background and understanding of the law. You get some interesting answers in these individual voir dire sessions. I have heard potential jurors say, "I don’t think I could give death to someone who killed in self-defense." That’s encouraging to hear, since killing in self-defense is not even a crime. I would hope no one could sentence a person to death for something that was not even criminal. Other potential jurors have said, "I could give it, but only if I witnessed the killing." You realize that if you did actually witness the killing, you would be a witness and not a juror, right? Same answer for those who said, "I could only give the death penalty to someone who killed a family member or a friend." Understandable, but you would be ineligible to serve on a jury if either of those were true.

In sum, capital cases are usually reserved for the worst offenders who commit murder plus an aggravating circumstance. For most of the cases in which I was involved, no one "gave" the defendant the death penalty. They earned it. It was a lifetime achievement award for raping, robbing and victimizing other people over the course of decades.

GAVIN NEWSOM WIPES OUT CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW IN HISTORIC MASS COMMUTATION

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is ineligible to serve on a death penalty jury. He claims he is morally opposed to the sentence, but more on his "morality" in a bit. He is likewise ineligible for extralegal reasons to be the chief executive of this country. In an act of reckless temerity, he cleaned out California’s death row. Five hundred forty-eight convicted murderers sentenced to death by California juries were let off death row by the governor on Nov. 5. As reported by Fox News Digital, the governor "will spare the lives of 548 inmates currently on the state’s death row, effectively clearing capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions."

Did Gov. Newsom do this when his name was on the ballot? Of course not; that would require conviction and principle. He did it on the way out the door when there would be no political fallout (or so he thinks).

CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

Did he consult the families of all the victims? Doubtful. Did he carve out exceptions for the most depraved inmates? Of course not. Did he carve out exceptions for those who had incurred additional infractions while incarcerated? By no means.

Even former President Joe Biden (presumably it was him) left the person who murdered nine Black Christians in a South Carolina church on federal death row.

HAWLEY ERUPTS AT BIDEN PARDON ATTORNEY OVER DYLANN ROOF CLEMENCY PUSH

Biden commuted 37 of the 40 federal inmates on death row. What he did is no less egregious than what Newsom did; it was just political pandering because of how public the killings of the three remaining inmates were. He left the man who killed nine Black Christians, he left the Boston Marathon bomber, and he left the man who killed 11 people at a Pittsburgh synagogue.

For all the talk about the rule of law, both men ignored it by singlehandedly overturning the will of 585 juries. Even allowing for the occasional bench trial in capital cases that represents overturning the will of thousands of women and men who had carefully weighed and balanced the aggravating and mitigating circumstances and found that the crimes committed so shocked the conscience as to warrant society’s ultimate punishment.

NEWSOM’S DEATH-ROW COMMUTATIONS SPARK DA REVOLT AS PROSECUTORS WARN OF LEGAL FIGHT

For all the talk about anti-democratic acts, what could be more anti-democratic than summarily overruling the will of people who sacrificed their time, their employment, and their innocence to listen to and view horrific fact patterns?

NEWSOM REVEALS WHEN HE'LL DECIDE ON 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID AMID GROWING SPECULATION

Were the men Newsom spared factually or legally innocent? Of course not. If they were, they would not have been on death row to begin with. If he believes any of those men were factually or legally innocent, he should have commuted their sentences long ago.

CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE'

Both Biden and Newsom waited until the last minute to undo what over 7,000 people had voted unanimously to do. People can have whatever views on capital punishment they want to have. That is none of my concern. I have family and friends who feel passionately on both sides of the issue. The more passion you have, the less likely you are to be trusted to serve dispassionately on a jury.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Newsom is a charlatan. His conscience is activated when he has one foot out the door and is seeking to run for higher office. That conscience was no doubt well-rested, as evidenced by the way he interacted with his (former) best friend’s wife and the way he flouted his own rules in the times of COVID.

I could not care less what Newsom’s opinion on capital punishment is. I do care when anyone overrules the vote of the people and summarily supplants their judgment with his own. That does damage to the rule of law and besmirches the memory of the lives lost in every one of the murder cases.

item.title: Illegal immigrant avoids charges after Florida grandmother killed outside grocery store, enraging family
item.description: Prosecutors dropped all charges against Carlos Suarez-Contreras in Deborah Murphy's death at a Panama City Beach Publix, citing hurdles under Florida law.
item.content:encoded:
The criminal case against an illegal immigrant accused of backing over and killing an elderly woman in a grocery store parking lot has been dismissed.

He will not face any charges for the accident, Larry Basford, state attorney for Florida’s Fourteenth Judicial Circuit, told Fox News Digital.

Several factors prevented prosecutors from pursuing and securing charges under Florida law, Basford said.

‘VIBRANT’ FLORIDA GRANDMA ALLEGEDLY KILLED BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT OUTSIDE PUBLIX, FAMILY FIGHTS FOR JUSTICE

"I think everyone would agree that what he did was careless and it was negligent," Basford said.

But, "not every tragedy amounts to a crime."

That’s heartbreaking news for the family of 82-year-old Deborah Murphy, said Murphy’s daughter, Amy Edge.

Both sets of tires crushed her body before the car stopped, she and her twin sister Beth Schulz told Fox News Digital.

THREE-TIME DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH KILLING NORTH CAROLINA GIRL, 6, AFTER RUNNING STOP SIGN

On May 17, Murphy walked back to her car carrying a bag after a brief stop at Publix in Panama City Beach. Surveillance video shows her striding through the crosswalk toward her car, when she was struck by a Toyota 4Runner moving in reverse, according to court records.

She was facing away from the vehicle as she walked, the video shows. She apparently didn’t see it coming.

FLORIDA DMV WORKER FACES 360 FELONIES FOR ALLEGEDLY HELPING ILLEGAL ALIENS GET LICENSES WITHOUT DRIVING TESTS

The driver, Carlos Suarez-Contreras, was a 26-year-old from Venezuela who was in the United States illegally, arrest records show. He was driving the vehicle with a canceled Georgia license, arrest records show.

Murphy was pushed to the ground by the SUV. But it didn’t stop.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCKER CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, 2 YOUNG SONS HEADING TO AIRPORT

The car continued backing up, "running over Ms. Murphy," according to an arrest affidavit submitted by the Florida Highway Patrol.

Suarez-Contreras was charged with driving with a canceled license and causing a death, a third-degree felony.

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER

He was held without bond because of his immigration status and because he was thought to be a "potential flight risk," Florida Highway Patrol records show.

Murphy was taken to the hospital and died from blunt force injuries less than an hour later, her daughters said.

Prosecutors worked on the case for almost six months, searching for answers that could lead to a conviction.

"We tried not to leave any stone unturned," Basford said.

ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

They found that Suarez-Contreras’ driver’s license had been canceled. But it became invalid only a day before the accident.

The Georgia Department of Driver Services confirmed to Fox News Digital that Suarez-Contreras' license had been canceled.

Citing privacy concerns, an agency spokeswoman would not say when it had been canceled, or when he would have been notified.

A non-U.S. citizen establishing residency in Georgia "must obtain a Georgia driver’s license within 30 days," according to the Georgia Department of Driver Services website.

A non-U.S. citizen is considered a resident if he or she "accepts employment or engages in trade in Georgia, and enrolls his or her children in a private or public school within ten days after the commencement of employment," according to the agency.

A person can also be considered a "resident" of Georgia if he or she is "present in the state for 30 or more days."

The question of whether Suarez-Contreras knew the license had been canceled is what proved problematic for prosecutors in Florida.

"Under the law, we have to prove that the individual knew his license was suspended," Basford said.

Prosecutors considered charging him with vehicular homicide and manslaughter, Basford said. But they couldn’t establish the culpable negligence needed for that.

Using the surveillance video that captured the fatal accident, investigators re-enacted the scene.

Considering that information, they decided the SUV wasn’t backing quickly enough to prove Suarez-Contreras was driving "recklessly" when he drove over Murphy.

At the scene, the passenger of the car, Luis Sanabria, gave sworn testimony to a law enforcement officer that it was Suarez-Contreras who "was operating the vehicle at the time of the crash."

Sanabria was found to have an expired visa, according to the incident report. He was released into the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Jacob Navarro, public affairs specialist for the Bay County Sheriff’s Office, told Fox News Digital.

In considering charges for Suarez-Contreras, prosecutors looked to a Florida law passed in 2023. It invalidates a driver’s license issued to an illegal immigrant in certain states, such as California, Connecticut and Delaware.

Unfortunately, the legislation does not designate Georgia as one of "those liberal states that gave licenses out so freely to individuals," Basford said.

Murphy’s family is devastated that there’s no chance of justice, Edge said.

"We feel incredibly let down by the state of Florida, who vowed to seek justice on her behalf," she said. "It's like experiencing the loss all over again."

Murphy was in great health and presumably had many more years with the family, Edge said.
Now, she won't attend her grandchildren’s weddings, or meet any more of her great-grandchildren, she said.

"That's been taken away."

Murphy’s two daughters are incredulous that Florida isn’t pursuing a trial. It could have set a new precedent for this type of case, Edge said.

At the beginning of the investigation the prosecution team had been very optimistic about securing multiple charges for Suarez-Contreras, she said. The only question in their minds at the time was the length of the prison sentence he would receive if convicted, she said.

She and her sister question the way their mother’s death was investigated and why so much weight was given to a re-enactment of the incident.

"We know the man killed her," Edge said. "He never got out of the car. He never ran to her aid. He never stopped. He wasn't reversing from a spot. He drove backwards."

The family also questions why Suarez-Contreras wasn’t tested for drugs or alcohol and why his phone records weren’t reviewed. Yet, Murphy’s body was subjected to a toxicology evaluation, her daughters said.

The sisters will continue to fight to bring positive changes from the tragedy. They may pursue changes to Florida law or the way law enforcement officers conduct similar investigations.

SEND US A TIP

"There's a lot of different questions we have that we'll continue to explore, but not in a vengeful way," Edge said. It’s "more in that we don't want this to happen to someone else."

GOT A TIP?

There’s some comfort knowing Suarez-Contreras is in ICE custody awaiting deportation, she said.

"We don't want him to be able to do this to anyone else in the United States. Our drive now is to ensure that he is deported."

Suarez-Contreras’ defense attorney, Russell Ramey, told Fox News Digital that he’s pleased the charges were dropped.

After the case was dropped, Suarez-Contreras was transferred into ICE custody on Nov. 15, according to the Bay County Jail. Fox News Digital could not reach him for comment.

item.title: NYC college put on notice after Jewish campus group shunned by student government: 'rude awakening'
item.description: Shabbos Kestenbaum decries anti-Jewish discrimination after a City University of New York school canceled a Cultural Arts Night, citing Title VI.
item.content:encoded:
A Jewish-American activist in New York City decried what he calls "anti-Jewish discrimination" after the student government at a school that is part of the City University of New York (CUNY) system, cancelled an event that was supposed to include the school's Hillel group when it received backlash from other student organizations.

Hunter College's undergraduate student government (USG) cancelled a "Cultural Arts Night" involving several student groups, including Hunter Hillel, the Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and the Center for Puerto Rican Studies, according to the New York Post. The radical far-left group Students for Justice Palestine was reportedly took part in planning the event.

In a statement to The Post, the school itself admitted that some of those groups withdrew from the event because Hunter Hillel was planning to participate.

JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS

"They were establishing a cultural arts night, which I might add also included countries with far worse civil rights violations like China, and none of that was a problem until, of course, the Jewish organization was involved," said Shabbos Kestenbaum, who described himself as a Jewish-American activist and who works for PragerU.

"So this is blatant anti-Jewish discrimination, and we as New Yorkers, we as Americans, and yes, we, as Jews, will do our best to hold the university accountable," he said.

The USG apologized for sponsoring the event, saying it had "failed" and that the event "should never have moved forward.

"To be clear, USG does not endorse this event or this collaboration, the apology said. "We hear what the student body has said, and we have made the decision to cancel the event as it doesn’t align with our values or the values of the students we represent as the Hunter Community. We apologize to the clubs and students who were affected by this instance."

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY

The apology said the group was actively working to ensure that such a mistake never happened again.

Kestenbaum believes that the school might have run afoul of anti-discrimination laws, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits any entity receiving federal funding from engaging in discrimination based on sex, race, ethnicity or other immutable characteristics.

He advocated for the federal government to pull its funding from Hunter College.

"It's just enforcing the laws already on the books," he said, adding that President Donald Trump and his administration have been making progress on punishing discriminatory behavior on college campuses.

"It's not something you pick and choose if you feel good that morning," he said. "It's the law and the expenditure of federal dollars is a representation of our values. And so if you're at university and you're discriminating against American citizens based on their ethnicity, based on the religion, based on their politics — not only is that a violation of law, but that's not a representation of where we want our money to go to."

Hunter Hillel responded to the cancellation in a statement to Fox News Digital.

BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS

"Hillel students were looking forward to taking part in the Cultural Arts Night, and our organization had no role in the student government’s decision to cancel it. Antisemitism has no place at Hunter College," the statement said. "The antisemitic response to the cancellation notice has been egregious and inappropriate. Rita Levine Rabin Hillel at Hunter remains committed to building joyful, strong, and vibrant Jewish life on campus."

Kestenbaum also referenced Rep.-elect Darializa Chevalier, D-N.Y., a prominent anti-Israel activist who took part in the infamous 2024 Columbia University encampment, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, himself a former anti-Israel activist.

He said students at New York's colleges are simply following the examples set for them by their elected officials.

CUNY has previously settled with the Department of Education after discrimination claims.

TRUMP ADMIN OPENS CIVIL RIGHTS PROBES INTO 15 COLLEGES OVER DEI GRANTS

"And all these elitist universities that think that they're higher and better than the law, they're in for a rude awakening," Kestenbaum said. "And again, you don't need to radically pass pieces of legislation that overhauls the bureaucracy. All you need to do is make it incredibly clear to these colleges, we are not giving you money if you discriminate. It is literally that simple."

The CUNY system did not return a request for comment.

"There is no place for discrimination and harassment in our college community," Hunter College told the New York Post. "We have policies in place to safeguard that principle and will not hesitate to enforce them."

Neither Hunter College nor its USG returned Fox News Digital's comment requests.

item.title: Forget what Randi Weingarten says, school choice didn’t hurt Republicans in midterms
item.description: Teachers union head Randi Weingarten says voters rejected school choice, but Greg Abbott's steady rural vote and 274,000 Texas applications tell a different story.
item.content:encoded:
Teachers union head Randi Weingarten and her teachers union allies are desperately trying to manufacture a narrative that Republicans lost ground in the midterms because of school choice. She said that "voters across the nation rejected the defunding of schools and the far-right’s culture wars and privatization agenda." The claim collapses under basic evidence.

Texas Democrat Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa took aim at school choice during her victory speech on election night when she said, "We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam."

Texas Democrats have already filed proposals to rip away scholarships from more than 100,000 mostly low-income kids right after campaigning on affordability. Most of the 10 Democrat Senate cosponsors either attended private school or sent their own children there.

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Demand for the program itself undercuts any claim of backlash. More than 274,000 students applied for Texas Education Freedom Accounts in the first year, with over 100,000 funded. Tens of thousands of families are on a waitlist after available funding ran out.

NBC exit polling from 2022 and 2026 shows Abbott received about the same percentage of the rural vote each election, between 64 and 66%. Gov. Greg Abbott held steady with rural voters in Texas even as his overall share of the vote shifted nine points to the left amid a nationwide blue wave.

DAN PATRICK CONCEDES TEXAS ‘TURNED PURPLE’ AFTER DEMOCRATS’ HISTORIC BLUE WAVE

If rural voters had turned on Abbott because of school choice, exit polling would have shown him losing ground with them. Yet he held steady with those families.

Education ranked near the bottom of voters’ top issues, well behind the economy and immigration.

BLUE WAVE MEETS BALLOT BOX SURPRISES AS VOTERS SPLIT ON ABORTION, VOTER ID AND BILLIONAIRE TAXES

And although more than 20 seats flipped from Republican to Democrat in the Texas House overall, only one of those flips occurred in the 30 most rural districts, which remained heavily Republican.

Texas voters rejected nearly $7 billion – about 85% of the total dollars considered on the ballot – in more money for the public school system this month. Texas voters overwhelmingly approved, 79.4% to a mere 20.6%, a ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption from school district property taxes just last year.

TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

Voters chose to reduce local taxes and associated revenue for public schools by a huge margin, undercutting any claim that they were clamoring for more money to put into the government school system or punishing Republicans over education policy.

A University of Texas at Austin poll conducted in October showed voters equally trusted the two gubernatorial candidates on public education. Democrats have historically held a double-digit advantage on the issue of education, so Hinojosa having a zero-point advantage suggests her education platform did not resonate with voters. A 2024 University of Houston poll showed 69% of Texas voters supported universal education savings accounts. University of Texas at Tyler polling also showed 60% support for school choice in 2023.

PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS

Eighty-eight percent of Texas Republican primary voters supported school choice on the 2022 ballot, and overall support was about the same for large and small counties. Republican primary voters overwhelmingly backed school-choice candidates in recent elections. In one example, in 2024, anti-school-choice incumbent Glenn Rogers lost his primary by 27 points.

The Dallas Morning News pushed propaganda from the teachers union by running an op-ed by "longtime Republican" Suzanne Bellsnyder that created a narrative that rural Republicans were embracing Hinojosa. The paper later added a note clarifying editors were not aware that Suzanne Bellsnyder’s firm was paid $57,000 by the Hinojosa campaign, and they would not have published the piece if they had known. The newspaper still refused to pull down the article entirely.

TEACHERS UNION SPENT NEARLY $8M TO CRUSH SCHOOL CHOICE, BIOLOGICAL SPORTS MEASURES, REPORT FINDS

The argument that school choice hurts rural communities fails on the merits. As school choice expands and brings more options to rural areas, families will have the choice to attend their district school. But they will no longer be resigned to it if the school is a poor fit. At the same time, competition is a rising tide that lifts all boats and improves public schools.

The oldest voucher programs in the country started in Maine and Vermont in the late 1800s specifically for kids in rural areas that did not have public schools. Over 150 years ago, these states figured out that not having a lot of options is a good reason to expand education opportunities, not restrict them. Those programs remain on the books today.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Mississippi and Alaska both flipped Senate seats to Democrats even though neither has a universal school-choice program. The leftward movement was national.

If anything, the evidence suggests Hinojosa might have won by more if she had sided with parents and supported school choice. School choice did not cost Abbott his election. But it might cost those now in power theirs in the future if they rip scholarships away from families who already have them. Once parents get school choice, they fight hard to keep it.

item.title: Jeffries calling Jerusalem NYC's ‘sixth borough’ resurfaces as progressives swing against Israel
item.description: Hakeem Jeffries once called Jerusalem the "6th Borough" in a resurfaced AIPAC clip, raising questions as he heads toward a January House speaker vote.
item.content:encoded:
Hakeem Jeffries once called his deep ties to Jerusalem an extension of his representation of New York City as he touted his support for Israel and the Jewish community.

But those comments from 2020, recently resurfaced and going viral, may come back to bite the Democratic House leader as the progressive wing of the party — and even some establishment members — continue to further break with U.S. maintaining support for the Jewish state.

"Someone said to me, ‘Hakeem, you’re going to Israel a 5th time?’" Jeffries recalled in an interview with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) more than six years ago.

"I said, ‘listen, I’m from New York City' — and back home in New York City, we consider Jerusalem to be the 6th Borough. And so, I’m just trying to catch up with my constituents."

The comments resurfaced just after he won his party's nomination to be speaker of the House in the next Congress.

JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES

The remarks from 2020 contrast starkly with a growing faction of the Democratic Party that has condemned AIPAC and the political favor Israel has historically enjoyed among lawmakers. The clip also raises questions over how far Jeffries will go to placate calls for a more critical review of U.S.-Israel relations in light of his previous support for the Jewish state.

Jeffries won a the secret-ballot vote to remain leader of the House’s Democratic Caucus with just 11 in the caucus voting against his leadership and 251 voting in favor. The result secured his nomination ahead of the full House floor vote in January, where he will need a simple majority of the chamber's 435 members to become Speaker.

During his AIPAC speech, Jeffries noted that some of his support stemmed from the uniquely challenging geopolitical environment around Israel.

"I think when you’re on the ground, for me it’s always been clear that Israel lives in an incredibly tough neighborhood," Jeffries said.

"When you think about the dangerous situation in the Sinai to the south, Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah to the north, Syria and chaos to the east, Iraq still a mess, Iran with nuclear ambitions and a tremendously bad actor — I grew up in Brooklyn in the late 80s and early 90s, I know from tough neighborhoods that Israel lives in a tough neighborhood," Jeffries said.

HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL

The stance clashes forcefully with at least eight members set to be a part of the 120th Congress with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group aims to "end all military and economic aid to Israel [and] prosecute U.S. and Israeli leaders responsible for the genocide in Gaza."

Two other members outside of the group, Democratic Reps.-elect Brad Lander and Scott Wiener have similarly called for a full embargo of Israel.

Jeffries’ own tone on Israel has changed over the years since the beginning of its war with Hamas in Gaza in October 2023, citing alarm at Israel’s civilian casualties.

In July, Jeffries argued in a letter to his colleagues that "a meaningful change in direction is needed."

"Israel has an advanced economy and is capable of paying for its own sophisticated weapons, as the Prime Minister recently acknowledged," Jeffries wrote.

"Accordingly, any future security arrangement between our two countries should be structured consistently with defense agreements that exist with our other Western allies and strictly adhere to our human rights laws and values," Jeffries wrote.

FETTERMAN WARNS THERE IS NO LONGER 'COMMON GROUND' WITH FAR-LEFT DEMOCRATS OVER ISRAEL

Even so, Jeffries has steered clear of calling the conflict a genocide — a growing characterization from within the progressive wing — and has rejected a blanket discontinuation of U.S. aid to Israel.

In his letter, Jeffries also condemned efforts from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to cut off all forms of assistance, advocating for a $3.3 billion military aid package to Israel included in the U.S. 2027 State Department appropriations bill.

"America’s commitment to Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish and democratic state and homeland for the Jewish people must remain ironclad," Jeffries said in his letter.

item.title: 6 vintage Thanksgiving recipes of decades past, from oyster stuffing to hot Dr Pepper
item.description: Creamed pearl onions, oyster stuffing and mincemeat pie once anchored Americans' holiday tables, says one chef, as vintage Thanksgiving recipes fade away.
item.content:encoded:
Before today's familiar lineup of Thanksgiving favorites, home cooks served rich and resourceful dishes and drinks that have largely disappeared from the holiday table.

While mashed potatoes, green bean casserole and mac and cheese might be some of the most popular dishes to pass around the table today, holiday menus of decades past transformed everyday pantry staples and convenience foods into celebratory recipes.

"Older Thanksgiving menus often included dishes such as creamed onions, oyster stuffing and mincemeat pie," Dennis Littley, a New Jersey-based chef and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital. 

THANKSGIVING DINNER KITS: 7 GROCERY CHAINS OFFERING HOLIDAY MEALS FOR UNDER $70

"Some have become less common as tastes and holiday menus have changed, though people still bring them back when they want to revive a family recipe."

Here's a look at six vintage recipes, including a warm, spiced soda drink.

Creamed pearl onions appeared in cookbooks as far back as 1896, according to online records, and were a familiar addition to Thanksgiving spreads by the 1920s, Taste of Home reported.

The dish pairs tender onions with a buttery white sauce similar to French béchamel. Frozen pearl onions later made it easier to prepare. The old-fashioned side still has devoted fans, according to Bon Appétit. Chef Thomas Keller has said his mother's creamed onions are a Thanksgiving dish he "can't live without."

5 FORGOTTEN ICE CREAM FLAVORS FROM THE '70S THAT FANS ARE BEGGING TO BE BROUGHT BACK

In a Reddit thread dedicated to old recipes, one person said his or her family still makes creamed onions today, carrying on a tradition from the person's great-grandmother.

Oyster dressing called for combining shucked oysters and their brine with classic stuffing ingredients including bread, celery and spices.

It was a Thanksgiving staple in the 1800s, when oysters were regularly available for purchase from refrigerated railcars, Food52 reported.

6 ICONIC AMERICAN RESTAURANTS STILL SERVING UP NOSTALGIA AND CLASSIC FLAVORS

The dish, with roots in British culinary traditions, fell out of favor in the Northeast as oyster populations declined and tastes shifted toward ingredients such as sausage.

Before pumpkin and apple pie solidified their place at the table, there was a meaty dessert contender. 

The filling of mincemeat pie was originally a sweet and savory mix of dried fruit, spices, citrus and meat — often beef or mutton — with suet, the fat of the meat.

"When we were kids my mom would always do mincemeat pie for both Thanksgiving and Christmas and we hated it," one commenter on Reddit recalled.

FROM FONDUE TO CASSEROLES: CLASSIC 1960S FOODS THAT DEFINED A GENERATION

Over time, meat disappeared from many recipes, leaving only the richly spiced fruit filling behind, though the pie's name still hints at its historic roots.

Long before Jell-O, cooks prepared savory aspics by simmering collagen-rich bones, skin and feet until the broth set, according to the Michelin Guide.

A labor-intensive showpiece once common in upscale French cuisine and wealthy households, aspic became more accessible with commercial gelatin and home refrigeration. 

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

By the mid-20th century, savory molds filled with meat, seafood, vegetables or hard-boiled eggs became a fashionable centerpiece at gatherings.

Aspics have made a recent comeback as home cooks explore nostalgic dishes and fine-dining chefs reimagine them as edible art, Fox News Digital previously reported.

The mayonnaise company Hellmann's promoted this molded holiday gelatin "salad" in a 1958 ad, according to reports. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Made with cranberry sauce, gelatin, mayonnaise, fruit and nuts, "Cranberry Souffle Salad" was chilled, whipped until fluffy and served on lettuce.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

A separate 1960 Hellmann's ad featured cranberry "candles," made with a similar mixture, molded in juice cans and topped with lit birthday candles, Bon Appétit reported.

In the 1950s and 1960s, Dr Pepper promoted the hot winter beverage, which called for heating the soda up to approximately 180 degrees Fahrenheit and then pouring it over a slice of lemon, as a way to boost sales during the slower winter months.

The idea originated in September 1958, when company president Wesby R. Parker visited a bottling plant during a blizzard and a salesman joked that they needed a hot beverage to sell during cold weather, according to the Dr Pepper Museum.

More festive versions even included rum, according to reports.

item.title: Harvard scientist may never prove mysterious space object’s origin after mission scrapped
item.description: Avi Loeb claims JAXA's canceled Hayabusa2 landing mission on 1998 KY26 ends the only chance to prove the object is the lost Soviet probe Phobos 1.
item.content:encoded:
A Harvard astrophysicist who claims a mysterious object speeding through our solar system is actually a lost Soviet spacecraft says scientists may never be able to get a clear look at it after Japan abruptly scrapped a planned mission to land on the target.

Avi Loeb told Fox News Digital that the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's decision to cancel its 2031 Hayabusa2 rendezvous with the object known as 1998 KY26 removes the only opportunity to capture high-resolution images of its surface and settle whether it is a natural space rock or the missing 1988 Soviet probe Phobos 1.

"There is no way by which we can actually resolve the object, or get a high-resolution image of its surface, without coming close to it — without a flyby — because even with the Webb telescope or the biggest telescopes we have on Earth, the object is not close enough to be resolved into multiple pixels in an image," Loeb said.

MYSTERIOUS OBJECT MOVING THROUGH SPACE COULD BE LOST SOVIET PROBE AS NASA WEIGHS IN ON THEORY

The cancellation came just days after NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman dismissed speculation about the roughly 36-foot-wide object during an appearance on "Fox & Friends," saying, "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is ... anything other than an asteroid."

Loeb pushed back on that assessment, arguing KY26 is "not an asteroid" because it accelerates in a way gravity alone cannot explain and predicting that when Japan's spacecraft lands on it in July 2031, scientists would find a label reading "Made in the USSR" instead of ice or rock.

NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS'

Japan's space agency reported to the Cabinet Office's Space Policy Committee on Nov. 16 that it was abandoning the 2031 rendezvous after the last normally functioning main ion engine on Hayabusa2 malfunctioned in mid-August, according to the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun.

"I was surprised that the cancellation by JAXA occurred just a day or two after I spoke about it publicly, because the malfunction in the engine was known for several months," Loeb said. "The probability that we're dealing with a coincidence where within a day after my public discourse, JAXA decides to cancel this mission is a day divided by the duration over which it was known that the fourth engine is malfunctioning – and that was over 100 days or so.

TRUMP HIGHLIGHTS NASA NUCLEAR-POWERED MARS SPACECRAFT MISSION PLANNED FOR 2028

"So, I would argue that the probability for a chance coincidence is less than 1%, but it could still be a coincidence," he added.

Loeb noted that Hayabusa2 was designed over several years and questioned why Japanese engineers did not attempt an Earth gravity-assist maneuver to compensate for the lost engine thrust rather than pivoting to another target.

JAXA officials said in their report that reaching KY26 in 2031 already required an Earth gravity assist, and that combining working parts from two damaged engines left the 12-year-old spacecraft without enough thrust to perform the necessary orbital changes, prompting a redirect to a 2028 flyby of asteroid 2015 BM510 instead, the newspaper added.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Even without a close-up flyby, Loeb said astronomers still have one major tool left to test his theory from afar by using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to measure the heat radiating off KY26 and analyze its chemical spectrum.

SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO

"So far, we detected a reflection of sunlight from this object, but the Webb telescope can potentially detect the heat emitted by the object, and that will offer us an opportunity to learn both about the size, the surface temperature of the object, as well as the composition of the object," Loeb said.

While mainstream scientists have suggested KY26 is an ordinary rock or comet, Loeb noted the object rotates about once every five minutes and is far brighter than expected.

EIFFEL TOWER-SIZED ASTEROID APOPHIS TO PASS CLOSER TO EARTH THAN MANY SATELLITES IN 2029, NASA SAYS

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"This object reflects about half of the sunlight that is impinging on it, whereas a typical rock or iceberg reflects about 5% of the sunlight impinging on it," Loeb said, adding that the object's brightness is "surprising."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

NASA previously told Fox News Digital that a 2025 orbital study led by the agency's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies concluded KY26's complex trajectory is driven by solar radiation forces – "the natural push of sunlight and thermal emission on its non-spherical shape" – rather than hidden comet-like activity.

SEND US A TIP

Loeb and his colleagues, however, found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of Phobos 1 – a Soviet spacecraft launched toward Mars in July 1988 that shut down after a faulty command – and calculated that sunlight reflecting off its solar panels could produce the observed push without any signs of a "dark comet" tail.

GOT A TIP?

"It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. "We should have seen the dust because for comets we see a tail and the dust particles are being pushed away from the sun by the solar radiation."

TRUMP SAYS AIR FORCE PILOTS DESCRIBED A ROUND UFO FLYING THREE TIMES FASTER THAN AN F-22 FIGHTER JET

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Loeb added that KY26 orbits the sun at a distance of a fraction to a few times the separation between Earth and the sun and poses no threat of hitting Earth, though he argued space agencies must remain open-minded when tracking unexplained objects.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

He noted that in January 2025, astronomers briefly cataloged an object near Earth as an asteroid before realizing it was actually the Tesla Roadster launched into space by SpaceX in 2018 – a mistake that was only caught because humans knew its flight path.

"Hopefully, the Rubin Observatory in Chile that is funded by the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation will find dozens of interstellar objects in the coming decade, and we should be curious enough to check whether all of them are rocks or icebergs, because if one of them is technological in origin, that will change our view on our place in the universe," Loeb said.

item.title: MAGA’s cool factor faces a test as Dallas Young Republicans confront midterm defeats
item.description: Dallas Young Republicans president Chad Cohen says the MAGA movement is still young and totally behind President Donald Trump, but fellow members are on the fence.
item.content:encoded:
Is it still cool to be MAGA? Dallas Young Republicans weighed in.

After Republican losses across the country in the 2026 midterm elections, young adults came together Tuesday to discuss what happened and how to move forward. Fox News Digital spoke with attendees and members about where they stand on the MAGA movement.

Chad Cohen, the president of Dallas Young Republicans (DYR), is confident that it is still cool to be MAGA.

"One hundred percent," Cohen said. "I think I speak for all of my members when I say we're still totally behind President Donald Trump. The MAGA movement is still early, it's still young."

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Cohen said the movement is looking for more politicians, like Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, Rep.-elect Jace Yarbrough, R-Texas, and Vice-President JD Vance.

However, not all members share Cohen's feelings. DYR member Mark said he is "on the fence."

"I'm a three-time Trump voter, but starting the new war with Iran was kind of a big letdown with this election," he said.

Ethan shared a very blunt assessment of the election and said the Republican Party needs to go in a different direction than MAGA.

"I would honestly say no at this point," he said. "I think in the 2026 midterm elections, Trump asked the people to come out and vote as if he was on the ballot, and people did. The 2026 midterms were a refutation of Trump."

DYR member Dan said whether or not it is still cool to be MAGA depends on "what your definition of MAGA is."

"I think after the midterms, we've seen some fragmentation within our party, which is part of the reason why we lost," he said. "I think people view there being two major factions, the MAGA party versus the American First Party. So I think our job as young Republicans here in one of the most conservative cities in the country to try to find a way to mobilize young people. To believe in the same vision that brought us together back in 2016."

VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY

Jack still believes it is cool to be MAGA.

"I think so," he said. "A lot of young men that run around in my crowd, I mean, we obviously still vote Republican, but I think a little bit of the young vote may have been lost due to social media, what's on there nowadays."

Jack added that the war in Iran was a big issue.

"I think the Iran war was a really big one ... impact to the MAGA message. I think that what it stands for at its core, especially like in the first term, what MAGA meant to us back then and what I voted for back then, I think it's still cool. I mean, in my circles, I think, it's true 100 percent."

Matthew Monfore, a political consultant and advisor who has spent time speaking to college students, doesn't think it is considered cool to be MAGA anymore based on what he has heard.

"Apparently not, what I'm seeing among conservatives on college campuses," he said.

TRUMP'S IRAN GAMBLE DIVIDES GOP HAWKS AND 'AMERICA FIRST' CONSERVATIVES OVER WHAT VICTORY LOOKS LIKE

Matthew said that supporting MAGA is neither good nor bad.

"I think at the heart of it, Make America Great Again was putting Americans first," he said. "And I think through the midterms, I think that a lot of people strayed away from putting Americans first as an American. I don't know if it's still considered to be good or bad. I think it's just at the heart of it, I think Republicans strayed away from putting the American party first."

Kai agreed that Make America Great Again is centered on putting America first.

"I think there's been a lot of hardships that we've all had to deal with just at a global scale, but when it comes down to the American people, I think putting the American first, especially from here on out," Kai said. "I think it's very important and I think that we can all be better for it if we choose to do so."

item.title: Kate Middleton's unexpected house rule for George, Charlotte and Louis: author
item.description: Like Queen Elizabeth II, who washed dishes at Balmoral, Kate Middleton uses chores, baking and gardening to keep her royal children grounded in normalcy.
item.content:encoded:
Being born into royalty doesn't mean getting a free pass at home.

Kate Middleton is reportedly determined to make sure Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis don't grow up expecting everything to be done for them. And the future queen consort has a surprisingly ordinary way of keeping her three children grounded.

It all starts in the family kitchen.

"When it comes to household chores, Kate is extremely organized," Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," told Fox News Digital, citing his own sources. Kate has made no secret of her fondness for one household chore in particular.

William was no stranger to getting his hands dirty before meeting his future wife.

During his gap year in Chile, the prince took part in charity work that involved chopping wood, making beds, washing dishes and doing laundry, Andersen said. The experience may have helped prepare him for the everyday household responsibilities he would later share with Kate.
